en: The *Saṃghāṭa Sūtra*, Scroll One.
Translated by Prince Yueposhouna of the Kingdom of Ujjayinī during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
Together with a great community of twenty-two thousand bhikṣus, whose names were:

the venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the venerable Śāriputra, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, the venerable Rāhula, the venerable Bakula, the venerable Bhadrasena, the venerable Kalyāṇabhadrika, the venerable Nandika, the venerable Jaṭila, the venerable Subhūti, and the venerable Nandasena;
together with these twenty-two thousand persons; and together with sixty-two thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, whose names were:

The Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra, the Bodhisattva Kumārabhūtaguṇa, the Bodhisattva Cittotpādakumāra, the Bodhisattva Kumārabhūtaketu, the Bodhisattva Anihīna, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, and the Bodhisattva Vajrasena—these and others, numbering sixty-two thousand, were all present together.
Furthermore, there were twelve thousand devaputras, whose names were:

the Devaputra Acyuta, the Devaputra Bhadra, the Devaputra Subhadra, the Devaputra Dharmakāma, the Devaputra Candanagarbha, and the Devaputra Candana; these twelve thousand devaputras were all together.
Furthermore, there were eight thousand devakanyās, whose names were:

He was accompanied by eight thousand celestial maidens, including the goddess Mṛṇālā, the goddess Sundarī, the goddess Mahāśaya, the goddess Śakunī, the goddess Lokapālinī, the goddess Balavatī, and the goddess Anuvartamānabāhu;
and he was further accompanied by eight thousand nāga kings, namely:

the nāga king Apalāla, the nāga king Elāpattra, the nāga king Timiṅgila, the nāga king Kuṃbhasaṃbhava, the nāga king Kuṃbhaśirīṣa, the nāga king Sunanda, the nāga king Susaṃkha, and the nāga king Gavaśirīṣa—these and others, numbering eight thousand nāga kings.

They all proceeded toward Vulture Peak to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound the True Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings.
World-Honored One!

Immeasurable billions of devas, immeasurable billions of celestial maidens, immeasurable billions of bodhisattvas, and immeasurable billions of śrāvakas have all gathered together, desiring to hear the True Dharma.
World-Honored One!
This great assembly all desires to hear the Dharma.
We only pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, will expound the sublime Dharma for us, so that we may be peaceful and secure throughout the long night and sever all karmic obstructions.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra:
“Excellent, excellent, Sarvaśūra!”
You have been able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such matters on behalf of the great assembly.
Listen attentively now!
Reflect upon it well!
"I shall explain it for you. "Very well,
World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra:
"There is a Dharma-gate named Saṃghāṭa."
If anyone in Jambudvīpa hears this Dharma-gate, they will be able to completely eliminate the karmic retribution of the five heinous crimes and attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Sarvaśūra! What do you think?
If a person hears this Dharma-gate, the mass of merit they acquire exceeds the mass of merit of a single Buddha.
Sarvaśūra addressed the Buddha, saying: “How is this so,
World-Honored One?”
The Buddha told Sarvaśūra:
"If a person hears this Dharma-gate, the merit they obtain will be equal to the merit possessed by as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are sands in the Ganges River."
"O Sarvaśūra! If anyone hears such a Dharma-gate, they shall never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they shall behold all Buddhas;
they shall all attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; evil Māras shall not trouble them, and all wholesome dharmas shall be fully accomplished."
"O Sarvashura!
Those who hear this Dharma will be able to know arising and ceasing.

At that time, the entire great assembly rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the measure of the merit of a single Buddha?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Listen attentively!

The merit of a single Buddha is like the drops of water in the great ocean, like the dust motes of the earth of Jambudvīpa, or like all sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, each of whom has become a bodhisattva of the tenth stage.
All the merit possessed by all Bodhisattvas of the ten stages is not equal to the mass of merit of a single Buddha.
Sarvashura! If a person hears this Dharma-gate, their merit will be greater than this, beyond the reach of calculation or analogy.
At that time, having heard these words, the entire great assembly leaped for joy and increased their merit and virtue manifold.
Then, the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Which sentient beings thirst for and delight in the true Dharma?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra: "Sarvaśūra!"
There are two types of sentient beings who thirst for and yearn after the Dharma. What are these two?
The first are those whose minds are impartial toward all sentient beings.
"Second, having heard the Dharma, they preach it equally to the assembly with no expectation of gain.
Sarvashura Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"By hearing what kind of Dharma does one draw near to Bodhi?
"Sarvaśūra! By thirsting for and yearning to hear the Dharma, one draws near to Bodhi."
"Those who always have faith and joy in hearing and receiving the Mahāyāna Dharma shall draw near to Bodhi.
At that time, humans, devas, nāgas, and celestial maidens rose from their seats.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We thirst for the Dharma; we pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will fulfill our wishes."

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled, and various colored rays of light issued from his mouth, illuminating the ten directions as far as the Brahma world, before returning and entering through the crown of his head.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition does the Tathāgata manifest this rare and extraordinary sign?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvashura:
"All sentient beings in this assembly shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and accomplish the realm of all Tathāgatas; for this reason, the Buddha smiles."
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions do the sentient beings in this assembly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Sarvashura!"
That you are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a meaning,
Sarvashura, is due to the excellence of your vows.

Sarvaśūra! In the past, incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Ratnaśrī Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
"Sarvaśūra! At that time, I was the son of a brahmin youth; those beings in this assembly who now abide in the wisdom of the Buddha were all, in former times, among the deer."
At that time, I made this vow:
"May all these deer be established by me within the wisdom of the Buddha.
Upon hearing this, the deer immediately raised their voices and said:
“May it be so! Sarvashura! By virtue of those roots of goodness, this great assembly shall attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma, for how many kalpas will their lifespan last?”
The Buddha said:
"That person's lifespan will last for a full eighty kalpas.
Sarvashura Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what measure is an eon defined?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! Suppose there were a great city, twelve yojanas in length and breadth and three yojanas in height, filled to the brim with sesame seeds.

A long-lived person were to come along once every hundred years and remove a single seed; in this manner, even when all the sesame seeds in the city have been exhausted, the kalpa would still not have ended.”
"Furthermore, Sarvashura!
Suppose there were a great mountain twenty-five yojanas in length and breadth and twelve yojanas in height.
If a long-lived person were to come once every hundred years and brush it with a single light silk cloth, even after the mountain had been worn away, the kalpa would not yet have ended."
"This is called the measure of a kalpa.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If even by making a single vow one obtains such a mass of merit and a lifespan of eighty kalpas, how much more so for one who extensively cultivates all practices within the Buddha-dharma?
O son of good family!"
If there are those who hear this Dharma-gate, their lifespan shall be full eighty kalpas, let alone those who copy it down, read it, or recite it.
Sarvashura!

If there is anyone who reads and recites this Dharma-door with pure faith, their merit will exceed that of the former; for ninety-five kalpas they will personally know their past lives, and for sixty thousand kalpas they will serve as a Wheel-Turning King.

In the present life, they will be honored by people; blades cannot harm them, poisons cannot injure them, and malevolent spells cannot take effect. At the time of death, they shall behold ninety-five billion Buddhas, who will comfort them, saying:
"Do not be afraid; during your life in the world, you heard the *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-gate."
"Ninety-five billion buddhas each took that person to their own world. Sarvaśūra!
How much more so for one who hears such a dharma-gate in its entirety!"
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If I were to hear and receive such a Dharma-gate as this, what merit would I obtain?”
The Buddha told Sarvaśūra:
"The merit possessed by as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River is exactly equal to the merit obtained by one who hears this sutra."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I listen to this Dharma, my mind knows no weariness.”
The Buddha said to Sarvashura:
"Excellent, excellent!
That you can thus listen to the Dharma without weariness—so too do I listen to the Dharma without weariness."
How much more so for ordinary beings who give rise to thoughts of revulsion! Sarvashura!

If there is a son of good family who hears this Dharma-gate and gives rise to faith, they shall not fall into the evil realms for a thousand kalpas; they shall not fall into the animal realm for five thousand kalpas; they shall not fall into ignorance for twelve thousand kalpas; they shall not be born in border regions for eighteen thousand kalpas; they shall be handsome in their place of birth for twenty thousand kalpas; they shall always attain renunciation for twenty-five thousand kalpas; they shall become kings of the True Dharma for fifty thousand kalpas; and they shall practice the mindfulness of death for sixty-five thousand kalpas.
"Sarvaśūra! Those good men and good women will have not the slightest unwholesomeness; evil Māras shall find no opportunity against them, and they shall not enter a mother’s womb."
“Sarvashura!

Those who hear this Dharma-gate will, in every place of rebirth, not fall into the evil realms for ninety-five *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. For eighty thousand kalpas they shall always attain the power of hearing and retaining; for one hundred thousand kalpas they shall be free from killing; for ninety-nine thousand kalpas they shall be free from false speech; and for thirteen thousand kalpas they shall be free from divisive speech.”
“Sarvashura!
Such a Dharma-gate is difficult to encounter and difficult to hear.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvashura rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How great is the offense of one who slanders this Dharma?
The Buddha told Sarvaśūra:
“Their transgressions are exceedingly great.
Then, the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"How many offenses does he incur?
The Buddha told Sarvaśūra:
"Do not ask about this matter."
"Good son!

If there were one who conceived an evil mind toward as many Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as there are grains of sand in twelve Ganges Rivers, and if there were another who slandered them, the latter's transgression would be greater than that."
“Sarvashura!
If one gives rise to a mind of malice toward the Mahayana, they will be scorched and consumed just like those sentient beings.
Sarvashura Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How can such sentient beings be saved?
The Buddha told Sarvaśūra:

“Suppose, for example, there were a person whose head had been severed by a blade, and a physician were to treat him by applying various medicines such as rock honey and clarified butter to the wound.
Sarvashura! [It would be the same.]”
"What do you think?
Could such a being be restored to life?
Sarvashura addressed the Buddha:
"No, World-Honored One! All-Vira! [he replied.
"All-Vira! [the Buddha said.]
Furthermore, it is like a person whose life is not severed by a blade, yet who recovers when treated by a skilled physician.
Once that person has recovered and realized the extent of their suffering, they think: "I have now understood; I shall never again commit evil or unwholesome deeds."
"Sarvaśūra! If a son of good family likewise reflects upon generosity in this way,
he will abandon all evil, gather all wholesome dharmas, and become fully endowed with all virtues."

Just as when a corpse has died, its parents grieve and weep but cannot rescue or protect it, so too are ordinary persons: they can neither benefit themselves nor others, and they have no parents to rely upon.
"So it is, so it is! Sarvashura!
Those sentient beings will have no refuge at the time of their death."
Sarvaśūra! There are two kinds of sentient beings who lack a refuge. What are these two?
First, those who commit unwholesome deeds;
second, those who slander the true Dharma—
these two types of persons have no place of refuge at the time of death.
Then the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
To what realm of existence are those who slander the Dharma reborn?”
The Buddha told Sarvaśūra:

"Those who slander the Dharma enter the great hells. They suffer for one kalpa in the Raurava Hell, one kalpa in the Saṃghāta Hell, one kalpa in the Tapana Hell, one kalpa in the Pratāpana Hell, one kalpa in the Kālasūtra Hell, one kalpa in the Avīci Hell, one kalpa in the Lomaharṣaṇa Hell, and one kalpa in the Huhuva Hell."
"Sarvaśūra! Those sentient beings who slander the Dharma shall undergo great suffering and affliction for a full eight kalpas within these eight great hells.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is great suffering, it is great suffering!
I cannot bear to hear it.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Why can you not hear?
These words are truly terrifying!"
Hell is a place of great suffering, where sentient beings endure agony.
If one performs wholesome deeds, there will be the retribution of happiness;
if one performs unwholesome deeds, one will receive the retribution of suffering.
Birth entails the suffering of death, bound by the sorrows of grief and lamentation;
ordinary beings constantly experience suffering, with not a moment of even slight joy.
Those of wisdom find happiness in being able to keep the Buddhas in mind.
"Having faith and purifying the Mahāyāna, one does not fall into the evil realms.
Thus it is, Sarvashura!
One obtains the retribution for one's original karma."
Though the labor performed is slight, one obtains boundless retribution;
though the seed sown is small, one obtains immeasurable fruit.
By planting seeds in the Buddha-field of merit, one is able to produce the harvest where fruits grow.
The wise attain peace and happiness, finding joy in all the Buddha-dharmas;
they remain far removed from the evil realms and practice all wholesome dharmas.
If one were to take even a single hair’s breadth of an object and offer it as a gift to the Buddhas;
For eighty thousand kalpas, he was immensely wealthy and possessed of riches and treasures.
In whatever place of birth he took, he always recollected the practice of giving.
Thus it is, Sarvashura!
"The merit gained from making an offering to the Buddha is profound.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvashura addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How does one cultivate the wisdom of a Buddha?
How does one hear this Dharma-gate and increase one's roots of goodness?
The Buddha told Sarvaśūra Bodhisattva:
"If there were someone who made offerings to as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in sixty-two billion Ganges Rivers, providing them with all manner of articles of pleasure;
and if another were to hear this Dharma-gate, the merit obtained by the latter would be exactly equal to that of the former."
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how are the roots of goodness fulfilled?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra, saying:
“One whose merit is equal to that of a Buddha should be known as one who has attained fulfillment.”
Sarvaśūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What person’s merit is equal to that of the Tathāgata?”
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra:
"Good son, the roots of merit of a Dharma-preacher are equal to those of a Tathāgata."
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said:
“World-Honored One,
who is this Dharma-preacher?”
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Sarvashura,
"One who circulates this Dharma-gate is called a Dharma-preacher.
The Bodhisattva Sarvashura addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What merit is obtained by hearing this Dharma-gate?
And how much merit is obtained by those who copy, read, and recite this Dharma-gate?”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra, saying: "Good son!

In the ten directions, in each direction there are Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of twelve Ganges Rivers; each and every Tathāgata remains in the world preaching the Dharma for a full twelve kalpas."
If there is a son of good family who expounds this Dharma-gate, his merit shall be equal to that of all the aforementioned Tathāgatas.
If there is a son of good family who transcribes this sutra, even forty-eight Ganges-sands of Buddhas and Tathāgatas could not exhaustively describe its merit;
how much more so for those who transcribe, read, recite, and uphold it.
Then the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra asked the Buddha,
“World-Honored One,
how much merit does one obtain by reading and reciting it?”
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with these verses:
"To recite and chant even a four-line verse Brings about this most supreme merit;
It is as [the merit from] eighty-four Ganges Rivers Of all the dharmas taught by the Buddhas."
By reading and reciting this Dharma-gate, one obtains such merit and virtue;
these various merits and virtues cannot be fully described by words.
Even if eighteen billion Buddhas were to remain in the world for a full kalpa, [they could not exhaustively describe them].
All Buddhas of the ten directions constantly praise the Mahāyāna Dharma;
they skillfully expound this Dharma-gate without end.
It is difficult to encounter the Buddhas, and this Dharma is likewise so.
At that time, eighty-four billion devaputras went to where the Buddha was, joined their palms in homage at his feet, and said to the Buddha: "Excellent,
World-Honored One!"
"May such a treasury of Dharma remain in Jambudvīpa.
At that time, there were another eighteen thousand billion Nirgranthas who came to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying: "Victory!"
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
The Buddha told the Nirgranthas:
"The Tathāgata is always victorious."
"You abide in perversion; how can you see yourselves as superior?
You have no superiority! Listen well!"
"Now, for your benefit, I shall speak to you:
'How can there be victory for an ordinary person who lacks wisdom?
Not knowing the True Path, how can there be victory?'"
"I behold the path of sentient beings with the exceedingly profound Buddha-eye.
At that time, the Nirgranthas conceived feelings of anger toward the World-Honored One.
At that time, Śakra took up his vajra-pestle and rubbed it with his hand, brandishing it at the Nirgranthas.
Then eighteen thousand billion Nirgrantha disciples were struck with terror and anguish, weeping and wailing piteously;
the Tathāgata concealed his form so that they could no longer see him.
At that time, the Nirgranthas, not seeing the Tathāgata, wept with grief and spoke in verse:
“Neither parents nor brothers Are able to provide rescue or relief.”
Seeing a vast wilderness and a great marsh, empty and devoid of people or paths;
there one finds no water, nor the shade of trees,
nor any multitude of men— alone without companions, one suffers misery.
“They undergo all these sufferings and afflictions because they do not see the Tathāgata.
Then the Nirgranthas rose from their seats, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and cried out in a loud voice:
“The Tathāgata, out of compassion, we pray that you will rescue us; we take refuge in the Buddha.”
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately smiled and addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra, saying:
"O son of good family!
"Go to the place where the heterodox Nirgranthas are and preach the Dharma for them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"Just as no small mountain can emerge above Sumeru, the king of mountains,
so too, World-Honored One,
I am unable to speak before the Tathāgata."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra:
"Good son, do not speak in such a manner; the Tathāgata possesses manifold skillful means."
Sarvaśūra! Go and observe all the worlds in the ten directions: where is the Tathāgata?
In what place does he abide, and where has he prepared the seat for the Tathāgata?
"Sarvaśūra! I shall also personally preach the Dharma among the Nirgranthas.
Sarvaśūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what spiritual power does he travel?
Does he go by his own spiritual power, or does he go by the Buddha’s spiritual power?”
The Buddha told Sarvaśūra:
"Go by means of your own supernatural power; when you return, come by means of the Buddha's supernatural power.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, prostrated before the Buddha, and immediately vanished from sight.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for the Nirgranthas:
"Birth is suffering and birth is affliction; human life is full of fear.
Birth brings the suffering of illness; illness brings the suffering of old age; and old age brings the suffering of death."
"Furthermore, there are the perils of kings, the perils of bandits, the perils of water, the perils of fire, the perils of poison,
and the perils of one's own past karma. At that time, the various non-Buddhists were filled with fear and said to the Buddha,
"World-Honored One!"
"We can no longer bear to live.
At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma, eighteen thousand *koṭis* of non-Buddhists were freed from dust and defilement and resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

There were eighteen thousand *koṭis* of great Bodhisattvas dwelling on the tenth stage, manifesting various supernatural powers of a Bodhisattva; some assumed the forms of elephants, horses, lions, tigers, or garuḍas; some took the form of Mount Sumeru; some appeared as old men; some as monkeys; and others sat cross-legged upon lotus pedestals.
Ten billion bodhisattvas were positioned on the southern side, and nine billion bodhisattvas were on the northern side; all of them performed such supernatural transformations and manifestations.
The Tathāgata constantly abides in samādhi, yet by the power of skillful means, he preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
At that time, the Tathāgata knew that Sarvashura Bodhisattva had departed by his own supernatural power and would reach the world of Padmottara after seven days.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, arrived at the place where the Buddha was in the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm. Having arrived, he circumambulated the Buddha three times to the right, generated a pure mind, joined his palms in salutation to the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
By means of my first supernatural power, I travel to the worlds of the Buddhas in the ten directions and behold ninety-nine thousand koṭis of Buddha-worlds.
By my second supernatural power, I behold one hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-worlds.
On the seventh day, I arrived at the world Padmottara and also reached the world of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.
World-Honored One!
Having reached that land, I beheld ninety-two thousand koṭis of Buddhas preaching the Dharma.

Furthermore, I saw eighty billion *koṭis* of worlds and eighty billion *koṭis* of Buddhas who on that very day attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; I made offerings to them all and then passed beyond.
“World-Honored One!

This very day I went to thirty-nine billion hundred-thousand Buddha-lands, where I saw thirty-nine billion hundred-thousand Bodhisattvas who had left the household life and attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
"Bhagavān!
I paid them all my respects and prostrations, circumambulated them three times to the right, and then departed.
Bhagavān!"
Furthermore, in sixty billion worlds, I saw sixty billion Buddhas; I made offerings to them all, paid them homage, and prostrated before them before departing.
World-Honored One!
I saw ten billion worlds where ten billion Tathāgatas entered parinirvāṇa; I likewise made offerings to them, paid them homage, and prostrated before them before passing on.
“World-Honored One!
I see that in sixty-five billion worlds, the True Dharma of the Buddhas has been extinguished; my heart is scorched with distress and I weep with sorrow.
I see devas, nāgas, and yakṣas grieving and wailing, as if arrows have pierced their hearts.”
“World-Honored One!
When that Buddha-world is consumed by the kalpa-fire, such that the great oceans and Mount Sumeru are all utterly incinerated without remainder, I too shall make offerings there and pass beyond;
then I shall arrive at the world named Flower-Adorned.”
“World-Honored One!
When I arrived in that world, I saw hundreds of thousands of billions of seats spread out.
World-Honored One!”
He saw that on the south side, hundreds of billions of seats were spread out; likewise, on the east, west, north, as well as above and below, hundreds of billions of high seats were each spread out.
"World-Honored One!
Each of those seats is composed of the seven treasures, and upon each seat sits a Tathāgata in the full lotus posture, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the assembly."
"Bhagavān!
Having seen this, a sense of wonder arose in me, and I asked that Bhagavān:
'What is the name of this world?'"
That Buddha-Tathāgata then addressed me, saying:
"This world is named Puṣpottara.
World-Honored One!

following him, there were successively twelve hundred million Buddhas, all of whom were named Ratnottama.
At that time, my name was Vimalacandra, and I practiced great generosity.
I made offerings to twelve hundred million Tathāgatas with robes, bedding, food and drink, medicinal elixirs, incense, flowers, lamps, and all manner of articles of pleasure;
yet those Tathāgatas did not bestow upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Sarvaśūra! I recall that in the past, eighteen billion Tathāgatas appeared in the world, all of whom were named Ratnaprabha.
At that time, I was named Nāgasamyak; I practiced great generosity, making offerings of fragrant flowers and necklaces to those Buddhas.
Those Tathāgatas also did not bestow upon me the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Sarvaśūra!
I recall that in the past, twenty billion Buddhas appeared in the world, all of whom were named Śikhin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
At that time, I practiced great generosity, making offerings of all manner of articles of pleasure to those Buddhas;
yet those Tathāgatas did not bestow upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Sarvaśūra! I recall that in the past, twenty billion Buddhas appeared in the world, all of whom were named Kāśyapa.
At that time, I practiced great generosity, making offerings to those Buddhas with various fragrant flowers, banners, canopies, robes, and all manner of musical instruments.
Those Tathāgatas also did not bestow upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Sarvaśūra!
I recall that in the past, sixteen billion Buddha-Tathāgatas appeared in the world, all of whom were named Viśuddhaprabha.
At that time, I was the son of a great elder, practicing great generosity by relinquishing all my possessions.
I made offerings to those sixteen billion Buddhas, Tathāgatas, with incense, flowers, banners, canopies, robes, bedding, food and drink, and medicinal elixirs;
yet they did not bestow upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Sarvaśūra! I recall that in the past, ninety-five billion Buddhas, Tathāgatas, arose in the world, all of whom were named Śākyamuni, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

At that time, I was a great king who ruled the world according to the Dharma. I made offerings to those ninety-five billion Śākyamuni Tathāgatas with incense, flowers, banners, canopies, food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and all manner of articles of pleasure;
yet they did not bestow upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Sarvaśūra! I recall that in the past, nine hundred million buddhas appeared in the world, all of whom were named Krakucchanda Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

At that time, I was the son of a brahmin, possessed of immeasurable wealth and practicing universal giving; I made offerings to the Buddhas with various fragrant flowers, banners, canopies, robes, bedding, food and drink, and all manner of articles of pleasure.
Yet those Tathāgatas did not bestow upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Sarvaśūra! I recall that in the past, eighteen billion Tathāgatas appeared in the world, all of whom were named Kanakamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."

At that time, I practiced great giving and made offerings to all those Tathāgatas, providing them with incense, flowers, banners, canopies, robes, bedding, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, and every kind of article of pleasure;
yet those Tathāgatas did not bestow upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Sarvaśūra! I recall that in the past, thirteen billion Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all named Prabhāśrī, appeared in the world.
I made offerings to them all, honoring and respecting them with various flowers, incense, banners, canopies, robes, bedding, food, drink, and every kind of article of pleasure;
yet those Tathāgatas did not bestow upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Sarvaśūra! I recall that in the past, twenty-five billion Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas appeared in the world, all of whom were named Puṣya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

At that time, I left the household life to practice as a śramaṇa, and I made offerings to those Tathāgatas in accordance with the Dharma, using various fragrant flowers, necklaces, banners and canopies, robes, bedding, food and drink, and all manner of articles of pleasure;
I honored and praised them, yet those Tathāgatas did not bestow upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Sarvaśūra! I recall that in the past, twelve billion Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all named Vipaśyin, appeared in the world.
I made offerings to all those Tathāgatas, providing them with flowers, incense, banners, canopies, robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and every kind of article of pleasure;
yet when I went forth into the homeless life, those Tathāgatas did not bestow upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Finally, when the Tathāgata Viśva spoke this Dharma-gate, as soon as the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa heard it, seven treasures rained down from the midst of space.
At that time, none of the sentient beings in Jambudvīpa were poor; yet even then, I did not receive the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"I merely heard a voice from the sky addressing me, saying:
'Before long, you shall receive the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Sarvashura Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
After how much time shall I receive the prediction of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra, saying:
"Listen attentively,
son of good family!
Ninety-two billion *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world, named Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
At that time, I was a māṇava named Megha—Megha meaning "Cloud" in the Wei language—who served as a māṇava under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and cultivated pure conduct.
I saw that Buddha making an offering of seven stalks of blue lotuses to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.
By means of these roots of goodness, he dedicated them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me this prediction: "Māṇava!
In the future, after an incalculable number of kalpas have passed, you shall attain Buddhahood and be known as Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."

"O Sarvaśūra! At that time, upon hearing the voice of the prophecy, I leaped into the air to a height of twelve tala trees; while dwelling in mid-air, I attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)."

The pure conduct cultivated over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, which accords with the six pāramitās, brings all roots of goodness to manifest before them, as clearly as looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand.
Sarvaśūra! At that time, I established immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of sentient beings in wholesome dharmas. Sarvaśūra!
How much more so now that I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and benefit sentient beings.
Observing by what means sentient beings should be delivered, I preach the Dharma for them according to their respective expedient means:
if it is for the sake of devas, I manifest a celestial body and preach the Dharma for them;
If among the dragon palaces, he manifests in the form of a dragon and preaches the Dharma for them;
among the yakṣas, he manifests in the form of a yakṣa and preaches the Dharma for them;
among the hungry ghosts, he takes the form of a hungry ghost and preaches the Dharma for them.
If they are to be guided by means of the human realm, he manifests in a human body and preaches the Dharma for them;
if they are to be transformed by means of a Buddha-body, he manifests in a Buddha-body and preaches the Dharma for them;
if they are to be transformed by means of a Bodhisattva-body, he manifests as a Bodhisattva-body and preaches the Dharma for them.
I observe by what means each sentient being should be delivered, and in such and such ways, I manifest for those beings and teach the Dharma according to their needs.
Sarvashura! I employ many skillful means to expound all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings.
Why is this? Sarvashura!
When sentient beings who are fully endowed with roots of goodness hear this Dharma, all their roots of goodness will increase.

The stingy practice generosity; those lacking merit cultivate merit; and for the sake of benefiting oneself and others, they cultivate mindfulness of death. Because they hear the Dharma, they produce these roots of goodness; and because they listen to the Dharma, their past roots of goodness also become further clarified. Thus, they shall obtain benefit and peace for all devas and humans throughout the long night.
"Sarvashura!
If this Dharma gate enters the ear but once, one will attain immeasurable merit. Sarvashura!"
At that time, sentient beings said to one another:
"Is there any other wholesome dharma through the practice of which one may attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
The virtuous sentient beings said:
"There are dharmas such as the practice of giving, the speaking of kind words, and so forth; through such dharmas, one attains the retribution of virtue up to the Unsurpassed Way."
Foolish people speak thus: "There is no dharma and no giving;
there are no fruits of good or evil, and no retribution for verbal virtue.
Those foolish people incur the retribution of great sin and, through successive rebirths, fall into the miserable realms.

For eight great kalpas, he fell into hell and underwent the retribution of great suffering; for sixteen kalpas, he fell among the asuras; for nine thousand kalpas, he was born among ghosts and spirits; for twelve kalpas, he fell among the hungry ghosts and underwent the sufferings of a hungry ghost; for fourteen thousand kalpas, he was born mute; for sixteen thousand kalpas, he miscarried from his mother’s womb; for twelve thousand kalpas, he was born as a mass of flesh; and for eleven thousand kalpas, he was born blind.
Those parents spoke thus:

"The child we bore has caused us to undergo toil and hardship in vain; for nine months we protected the fetus, fully enduring all sufferings such as hunger, thirst, cold, and heat, yet we have not obtained the power of the child’s gratitude."

"Thus it is, Thus it is, Sarvaśūra! Sentient beings who slander the Dharma fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; at the moment of death, they depart pierced by the arrows of anxiety and distress."
Sarvaśūra! Those who speak well with their mouths say:
"There are dharmas; there is giving; and there are the fruits and retributions of wholesome and unwholesome karma."

By reason of these roots of goodness, that person will be reborn in Uttarakuru for twenty-five kalpas; for twenty-five kalpas they will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to enjoy the various celestial pleasures. When their life in heaven ends, they will be reborn in Uttarakuru. They shall not enter a mother’s womb, but will see hundreds of thousands of worlds with their own eyes, all named "Peaceful Bliss. They will behold the Buddhas of all lands without ever leaving their original place, and they will attain perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
Sarvaśūra! This Dharma-gate possesses great supernatural power; it can inspire pure faith, prevent one from being born in the borderlands, and cause one to be endowed with pure precepts.
“Sarvaśūra! Furthermore, there are sentient beings who speak thus:
‘The Tathāgata delivers all sentient beings day and night; yet why is it that the realm of sentient beings is still not exhausted?’”

Innumerable sentient beings aspire to enlightenment; innumerable sentient beings are born in the heavens; innumerable sentient beings enter parinirvāṇa—by what causes and conditions do they not come to an end?
Then the various non-Buddhist brahmins and others spoke these words:
"We shall challenge the śramaṇa Gautama with such difficult questions regarding this meaning.
At that time, ninety-four billion non-Buddhist brahmins and others came to the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled radiantly.
Then, the Bodhisattva Maitreya—*Maitreya* meaning "Compassion" in the Wei language—rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
For what cause and condition does the Tathāgata smile?
Without a cause and condition, the Tathāgata never manifests such a rare event.
We pray that the World-Honored One will explain: for what reason has he manifested this smile?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya: "Good son!
Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you."
“Maitreya! Today there will surely be a great assembly gathered in the city of Rājagṛha.
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What assembly has gathered?
Is it devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, or non-humans?”
The Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "Good son!
All these devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and others have gathered here."
Furthermore, eighty-four thousand brahmins and nine hundred billion nirgranthas came desiring to engage in debate.
I completely subdued all those brahmins and preached the Dharma for them, causing them all to resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Nine thousand billion Nirgranthas all attained the *srotāpanna* (in the Wei language, "逆流," meaning "逆流" or "flowing against the current").
Eighteen thousand billion dragon kings all came to the assembly; having heard me preach the Dharma, they all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Sixty trillion devas from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens also came to the assembly; furthermore, thirty trillion Māras along with their retinues also came to the assembly; twelve thousand asura kings all came to the assembly; and five hundred great kings together with their retinues all came to the assembly to hear me preach the Dharma.
"Having heard the Dharma, they all resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Maitreya rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then vanished from sight.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"What are the names of those five hundred kings?
The Buddha told Sarvaśūra:
"Listen attentively!"
Good son! First is named King of Joy;
second is named King of Excellent Joy.
Third, named King Upananda;
fourth, named King Jayottara;
fifth, named King Brahmasena.
Sixth, named King Brahmaghoṣa;
seventh, named King Sudarśana;
eighth, named King Suprīti.
Ninth, named King Prītikara;
tenth, named King Samyakprīti;
eleventh, named King Bimbisāra.
Twelfth, King Prasenajit; thirteenth, King Virūḍhaka.
There were five hundred such great kings, each with a retinue of ten billion followers, all of whom resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, with the sole exception of King Virūḍhaka.

From the east, thirty trillion bodhisattvas came together in assembly; from the south, fifty trillion bodhisattvas came together in assembly; from the west, sixty trillion bodhisattvas came together in assembly; from the north, eighty trillion bodhisattvas came together in assembly; from below, ninety trillion bodhisattvas came together in assembly; and from above, one hundred thousand billion bodhisattvas came together in assembly.

All those bodhisattvas dwelt in the ten stages; they all proceeded to the great city of Rājagṛha and arrived at the place of the Tathāgata, having attained non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra, saying:
"Good son! Go to the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions and tell all the bodhisattvas there:”
"Today the Tathāgata is expounding the Great Dharma in the city of Rājagṛha; you Bodhisattvas from the ten directions should join your palms in reverent worship.
Return quickly in an instant so that you may listen to the Dharma together with this assembly.
At that time, Sarvaśūra Bodhisattva rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and suddenly vanished.
Then, the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra went to the lands of the ten directions and addressed the bodhisattvas there, saying:
"Today, the Tathāgata is expounding the Great Dharma in the city of Rājagṛha; you should now praise it as excellent, so that you may forever attain peace, happiness, and benefit."
At that time, Sarvashura Bodhisattva went to the lands of the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas; having finished instructing the bodhisattvas there, he returned to this land.
In the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and stood before the Tathāgata.

At that time, all the brahmins and various non-Buddhist practitioners had already assembled; devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, humans, and non-humans had all gathered together; five hundred great kings along with their retinues had also come to assemble; and thirty trillion evil Māras along with their retinues had likewise come to assemble.

At that time, the earth of Rājagṛha city shook violently. Simultaneously, throughout the worlds of the Buddhas in the ten directions, powdered sandalwood incense rained down, as did exquisite celestial flowers. These fell upon the Tathāgata, forming great flower pedestals. The Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattvas stood before the Tathāgata, each grasping a vajra-pestle.

At that time, there were four Wind Kings from the four directions who entered the city of Rājagṛha and blew away all the filth, excrement, soil, and sand within the city, casting them far outside the city walls.

At that time, fragrant waters rained down upon the worlds of the ten directions; furthermore, blue lotuses (utpala), yellow lotuses (kumuda), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka) rained down from the worlds of the ten directions, transforming into flower canopies suspended in mid-air.
In the void of space, there were eighty-four trillion lion thrones made of the seven precious gems; upon every throne, a Tathāgata was proclaiming the sublime Dharma.
At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition has a rare event manifested in the city of Rājagṛha?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra:
"O son of good family!"
Listen well now!

Suppose there is a person who, out of self-conceit and pride, goes to the gate of a king’s palace while his own home is in poverty. Having arrived at the gate, he enters directly with haughty arrogance; then the gatekeeper seizes him, beats him, and binds him.
When the king heard that someone had entered the royal gate directly, he thought to himself:
"This person has entered straight in; they surely intend to harm me.
At that time, the king, filled with wrath, commanded his ministers, saying:
"Take this man and sever his life-force, along with his father, mother, brothers, and sisters.
Thereupon, the man's kinsmen were all filled with grief and sorrow, weeping and wailing aloud.

The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is also like this: those who are self-attached and arrogant are likened to ordinary worldlings; though they see the Buddha’s body and hear his preaching of the Dharma, they give rise to pride within themselves and utter various words. Dwelling on the ground of self-attachment, they neither listen and receive the teaching for themselves nor preach the Dharma to others.
If a person hears someone preach even a single verse or a single parable and does not listen or accept it,
saying instead: "I already knew this Dharma before," why is that?

Abiding on the ground of self-conceit, or relying on their extensive learning to indulge in negligence, they dwell together with foolish people and do not hear the True Dharma. Out of pride in their own learning, they speak negligently and unrighteously; they compose their own writings and then preach them themselves.
All people in the world deceive themselves by saying such things as:
"Give wealth to me; I am a field of merit.
Those foolish people deceive themselves and also deceive the world; because they cannot digest the offerings of others' faith, they give rise to great terror when their lives are about to end.
The people said to him, "You possess great skill; why do you not save yourself?
He replied:
"Today, despite our skills and arts, we cannot save ourselves from this sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
The crowd said:
"For the sake of one person, parents, brothers, kinsmen, and relatives are being slaughtered for no reason."
"In this way, sentient beings who associate with evil friends fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
It is so, it is so! O brahmins and nirgranthas!"
I now tell you: do not be negligent.
Just as a fledgling bird that has not yet grown its wings cannot soar high into the void, so too you, lacking such divine power, cannot fly to the realm of Nirvana.
Why is this? The Dharma you practice is not the ultimate path; it will ultimately end in destruction.
At the time of your death, you will yourselves give rise to a mind of regret, saying:

"We have received this body and life in vain; we practice without attaining celestial bliss, without enjoying human happiness, and without attaining nirvana. Thus, this body of ours has passed away to no purpose."
"To what realm shall I be born?
What kind of body shall I receive?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmins, the Nirgranthas, and all the other non-Buddhist practitioners, saying:

“Jambudvīpa is filled with precious treasures; do not let your hopes be frustrated. Do not pursue heterodox paths within the jewel of the Buddha’s Dharma. Ask the Tathāgata about whatever you doubt, and the Buddha shall analyze and explain it for you.”

At that time, all the brahmins, nirgranthas, and others rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, joined their palms in homage to the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata delivers sentient beings from birth and death many times throughout the day and night, yet the realm of sentient beings neither decreases nor increases.
World-Honored One, for what cause and condition do these sentient beings undergo birth and extinction?

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, adorned with great vows, desiring to kindle the torch of the Dharma and inquire about a matter of great importance, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"In future ages, there will be no small sentient beings and no old sentient beings who undergo birth and death.
The Buddha told Bhaiṣajyasamudgata:
"Sentient beings become small through aging; such is their birth and death."
"Good son!
It is like a person who, having washed his hair and put on new clothes, goes out from his house, and another person says to him:
'Well-washed is your hair; you wear these new, clean garments.'"
"Furthermore, it is like a person who washes their hair and puts on old, washed clothes; though the hair is well-washed, the clothing is not fine.
Just so, just so, O Bhaiṣajyasamudgata!"
"Among sentient beings, those who are old are considered not wonderful in Jambudvīpa, while those who are young, though wonderful, are seen to possess birth and extinction.
At that time, all the brahmins and the various non-Buddhist Nirgranthas said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is called 'old,' and who is 'young'?
The Buddha addressed the non-Buddhist practitioners:
"What is called 'old age' means repeatedly coming and going among hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings, undergoing suffering without ever reaching satiety.
At that time, all the brahmins, devas, nāgas, and great kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We can no longer endure the suffering and affliction of birth and death.
Those Nirgranthas spoke these words:
"There are no small sentient beings."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Observe how difficult it is for these sentient beings to be delivered.”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja:
"The Tathāgata shall now provide a detailed explanation; listen attentively!
There are ninety-four trillion newly initiated sentient beings who, standing before the Tathāgata, neither prostrate to the Tathāgata nor offer him greetings."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what cause and condition do these sentient beings not pay homage to the Tathāgata?”
Nor did you inquire after his well-being or request a resolution for your doubts?
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja: “Good son!
Listen attentively now!
I shall explain it for you. Noble son!
If one were to say that there are no "small sentient beings," such a person is himself a small sentient being.
That person will then ask:
"We people are small sentient beings."
“World-Honored One!
We are but small beings.
The Buddha said:
"It is so, it is so. You are but small beings,
for you are unable to know the measure of your own selves."
At that time, ninety-four trillion newly initiated sentient beings all attained the tenth stage and dwelt in the void.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
These sentient beings have swiftly attained great benefit by bringing an end to birth and death.
World-Honored One!
These sentient beings, having departed from birth and death, abide in the tenth stage.
At that time, all the brahmins, the various non-Buddhist Nirgranthas, the dragon kings, and the retinues of Māra came to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We have come to the Buddha to hear this Dharma-gate; may we all obtain a body of wondrous form and color like that of the Tathāgata, and may we become like the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is!
Son of good family!"
Come to the presence of the Buddha and listen to this Dharma-gate; arouse the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and you shall before long attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

When the Tathāgata had spoken these words, all the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas and others attained the stage of endurance in the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and dwelt in the tenth bhūmi.

At that time, the bodhisattvas, by means of their own supernatural powers, leaped into the air to a height of seven tala trees; in mid-air they transformed themselves into palaces made of the seven precious jewels and offered them to the Tathāgata, performing various supernatural transformations while suspended in the sky.

At that time, the devas in the midst of the void, above the Tathāgata, rained down various wonderful flowers; they recollected the Tathāgata and conceived the perception of the Buddha’s body within their own bodies.
Countless hundreds of thousands of devaputras scattered flowers over the Buddha and spoke these words:

"We have gained great benefit! The śramaṇa Gautama is truly a great and excellent field of merit for the world; he is fully endowed with the power of mastery in samādhi. For such beings as these, he gradually provides the skillful means, so that by uttering a single word of goodness, they may escape birth and death."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition do these sons of the gods speak such words, manifesting various supernatural powers and skillfully praising the Tathāgata?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, saying: "Good son!"

Those bodhisattvas do not praise me, but rather praise their own bodies; for they themselves sit upon the throne of the Dharma King, they themselves sit upon the Dharma seat, and they themselves emit the radiance of the Dharma. Protected by all Buddhas, they realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and preach the Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Greatly Virtuous World-Honored One!”
Day and night he constantly delivers immeasurable sentient beings, yet these sentient beings remain inexhaustible.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, saying:

The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, saying: "Good son!

"O Bhaiṣajyasamudgata!

“World-Honored One!
How does death arrive?

Good son!”
"These three kinds of winds stir the active consciousness at the time of death.

"World-Honored One!"
"What are the three dharmas that afflict the body-consciousness at the time of death?

First, the affliction of knives;
second, the affliction of needles;

"These three kinds of winds afflict and torment his body.
That young being addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“What is this body?
The Buddha said, “Good son!

The body is called a mass of fire; the body is called burning; the body is called delusion; the body is called collapse and ruin; the body is called a thicket of thorns; the body is called a burial mound; the body is called a water bubble; the body is called a heavy burden; the body is called the arising of affliction; the body is called old age, sickness, and suffering; the body is called death, separation from the beloved, and encountering the hated—this is what is called the body.
Those youths spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is this body called 'death'?"
"What is meant by 'arising'?
The Buddha said, "Good son!
The cessation of consciousness is called death;
the arising of consciousness through the causes and conditions of merit is called birth. Good son!
That which is called the body consists of immeasurable billions of sinews and veins intertwined; the body has eighty-four thousand pores, and within them dwell eighty-four thousand families of worms.
Those various worms also undergo death and extinction.
When a person is about to die, the worms become terrified; they devour one another and experience manifold sufferings and pains.
The male and female kinsmen give rise to great sorrow and distress as they devour one another.

Among the various insects that feed on each other, there are only two insects who fight for seven days; once the seven days have passed, one insect’s life comes to an end while the other still remains, just like those fighting insects who do not cease even when facing death.

Ordinary people are just like this: even as they approach the end of their lives, they do not cease their disputes; they do not fear the suffering of birth, they do not fear the suffering of old age, they do not fear the suffering of illness, and they do not fear the suffering of death—just like those two insects that do not cease until death.
Ordinary worldlings are just like this: when death arrives, the noble ones rebuke them, saying, "O man!
You have committed unwholesome deeds; do you not see the suffering in the world?"
"I do not see the suffering of birth, I do not see the suffering of illness, I do not see the suffering of old age, and I do not see the suffering of death.
He replied, "It is so;
I have already seen the suffering of birth, the suffering of illness, the suffering of old age, and the suffering of death."
"If you perceive such suffering as this, why do you not cultivate the various roots of goodness?
For what reason do you not practice the various wholesome dharmas for the sake of happiness in future lives? O man!"
I ask you again:
Why do you not perform wholesome deeds to free yourself from the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, and the suffering of death?
Why do you not cultivate the contemplation of right mindfulness?
Have you not heard the sound of the ghaṇṭā in Jambudvīpa?
Have you not seen sentient beings practicing generosity?

Have you not seen sentient beings planting the seeds of roots of goodness in the field of merit of the Buddha—did you not see them when they offered incense, flowers, banners, and canopies to the Buddha?
The Tathāgata has four assemblies of disciples—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—who, within the Buddha-dharma, are able to rescue these four assemblies from suffering and calamity.
The noble sages rebuked him, saying:
"O unwholesome man, you have committed such an unwholesome deed. At that time, the Dharma King spoke in verse, saying:
"Having seen the Tathāgata appear in the world, And having heard the sound of the Dharma drum being struck;..."
Seeing the teaching of the Dharma being proclaimed, which leads to the peace of Nirvana;
seeing that among many sentient beings, those who perform meritorious deeds are very few—
since merit brings happiness in future lives, why do you not practice it?
At that time, the man replied to the Dharma King in verse:
"I was foolish and lacked wisdom; I associated with evil friends;
I committed unwholesome deeds, My mind being deluded by desire."
Because I indulged excessively in sensual desires, I now receive this retribution of suffering and pain;
because I killed many sentient beings, disrupted the harmony of the Saṃgha,
and destroyed Buddhist stūpas and monasteries.
Foolish and lacking wisdom, I spoke unwholesome words with my mouth, reviling my parents.
Through my lack of awareness, I have committed many transgressions myself.
I have seen the places where I was born: in the Great Howling Hell and in the Hell of Collapsing Mountains, I underwent great agony;
furthermore, in the Avīci Hell, I endured immeasurable and intense suffering.
In the Great Lotus Hell, one undergoes immeasurable suffering;
in the Black Rope Great Hell, one suffers for hundreds of thousands of lifetimes;
in all the hells, one universally experiences every kind of torment.
For countless hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they endure great agony;
wandering through the dark hells, they cannot see their exits.
They fall again into cauldrons of fire, undergoing manifold sufferings as they are tossed about.
Furthermore, there is another hell named the Sword-and-Spear Hell;
hundreds of billions of swords and spears stand in rows before me,
cutting and slicing my body as I suffer the torments of my own karma.
Not fashioned by a craftsman, but born spontaneously through the retribution of karma;
stirred up by great winds, it cuts and lacerates my entire body.
I must endure such various sufferings and afflictions of hell.
All sentient beings see me undergoing this suffering.
All the wealth and treasures I possess remain entirely in this world;
so too do my sons and daughters, brothers, sisters, and kinsmen.
Parents and kinsmen, slaves and laborers; cattle, sheep,
and all manner of livestock— in these my mind was deluded,
greedily attached to gold, silver, and jewels, as well as exquisite garments.
Clinging with greed to the construction of houses, With skilled artisans as painters of dwellings,
And the pleasures of many maidens, Along with the sounds of kōnō, flutes, and pipes—
Those of deluded mind, with these, Bathe themselves in fragrant waters.
Thus one amuses oneself, providing various offerings to this dull, ignorant, and witless body;
with a mind of false attachment, one today undergoes immeasurable suffering.
Suffering is inexhaustible.
Clinging with greed, they devour; they smear fragrant oils upon their hair and wear jeweled garlands, intoxicated by their own lust for form.
Now there is no one to provide rescue;
the eye is the cause of evil karma, for upon seeing, greed arises; the ear is the cause of various sounds, for upon hearing, greed arises.
On her fingers she wears golden jeweled rings; on her throat and neck she wears jeweled necklaces;
on her feet she wears golden bracelets;
she has fashioned a golden jeweled net that covers her body like a canopy, and her person is adorned with various kinds of jewels.
Adorning themselves with these as the foremost ornaments in the world, they take them as bodily adornments;
thus they increase their craving for sensual desires, using various exquisite couches and seats.
They delight their own bodies with various excellent and wondrous fragrances;
they smear their own bodies with sandalwood and camphor incense.
Using various perfumes such as musk, he anoints his own body;
with *campaka* and *sumana* flowers, he adorns his hair;
wearing the most exquisite and refined garments, he clothes his body in white cotton cloth.
If he abandons his white elephant mount and instead rides upon horse-drawn carriages;
if he governs the state as king and is held in high esteem by all the people;
and if the various queens and consorts within the palace are skilled in song, dance, and performance.
Wild beasts in the wilderness have no reason to hunt and harm;
yet they commit such evils as these, unaware of the retribution in future lives.
Because they devour the flesh of others, they undergo such bitter retribution.
Foolish and devoid of wisdom, they do not know that death must come;
though they nourish their physical lives, today they arrive at the gate of death,
and none can provide rescue.
"You, my kinsmen, what use is it for you to look upon me?
Why do you not put on fine garments?
For what reason do you grieve and weep?"
Why do you not shave your hair,
yet undergo such suffering?
Because you have committed many evils, you become foxes, wolves, crows, magpies, and the like.
"Eat the flesh of this body of mine;
nourish this physical form, for it is already being devoured by various worms.
Sentient beings are thus subject to birth; one should administer medicine in this manner."
May they be enabled to escape this hardship.
Where worldly physicians cannot heal and no one is there to provide rescue,
today I bestow the medicine of the Dharma to extinguish the disease of afflictions.
Though this body is nourished in various ways, it must inevitably return to death;
yet the Unsurpassed Honored One of the world saves all sentient beings,
and the sons of the Buddhas who dwell in tranquility can likewise save sentient beings.
Bestow the medicine of the sublime Dharma to bring about liberation from birth and death.
By eating meat, one nourishes this body and remains ignorant of its various bitter retributions;
to nurture this body yields not the slightest benefit.
This body is a mass of dullness and ignorance, unaware of even a small measure of kindness;
wives, concubines, sons, daughters, and the like do not recognize the power of their own indebtedness.
Having been nurtured until full growth, there is none who can provide rescue;
despairing and without knowledge, one enters the realm of death in sorrow.
For sentient beings there is the suffering of birth, and thereafter the suffering of death.
Perception, mental formations, contact, sensation, and so forth—these constitute middle suffering.
Bound by ignorance and craving, one is born into the various realms of existence;
fettered by desire and lust, one takes pleasure and attachment in sensory objects.
Because sentient beings lack wisdom, they possess only sorrow, affliction, and suffering;
not recognizing wholesome dharmas, their minds cling only to names.
They do not know of the future life, which is like a venomous serpent.
Ignorance turns sentient beings away from liberation;
because they do not recognize liberation, they are driven by evil karma.
Because their minds are possessed of afflictions, sentient beings dwell in birth and death.
Afflictions incinerate all wholesome virtues, just as fire consumes dry wood;
one wanders through the five realms of existence without experiencing even the slightest pleasure.
One does not know where that excellent and wondrous bliss might be found.
