as your bodily form is free from all unwholesome dharmas, and as we see your palms adorned with the seven treasures and your body draped in jeweled necklaces—a mass of merit—we do not know what kind of person you are."

"We have no need for food, nor do we need drink; for when food enters the body, it is utterly loathsome, transforming into excrement and urine, and forming flesh, blood, sinews, and skin. Therefore, we have no need for food or drink."
One has no need for any fine or soft garments, nor for armlets, golden bracelets, pearls, necklaces, or any ornaments for adorning the body, as these are all subject to impermanence.

We, too, do not begrudge our bodies or lives; we seek the gift of Dharma in order to leave the evil realms behind, to bring peace and happiness to devas and humans, and to seek out virtuous friends. We do not seek to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, for although a Wheel-Turning King rules over the four quarters, he cannot escape decay and extinction. His sons, daughters, wives, and children cannot follow him; his seven treasures will not accompany him, nor will his immeasurable multitudes of subjects. Over the four continents, he will no longer possess sovereignty.

Having served as a king throughout many lifetimes, you have witnessed much impermanence; because of the evil karma you created, you have fallen into the Raurava Hell. Where now are the four continents over which you once traveled with sovereign mastery of the seven treasures?
"O Benevolent One!
Listen to what we say and quickly go to the presence of the Buddha.
The Buddha observes all beings and regards them with compassion as his own children; for us, there is no father, no mother, no brothers, and no kinsmen—nothing at all."
The Buddha is my father, and the Tathāgata is my mother.
Like the sun and moon, the Buddha reveals the path of goodness to humanity; within the cycle of birth and death, he can rescue sentient beings so that they shall not be born again.
The rivers of all afflictions are most terrifying; sentient beings are adrift and drowning within them, yet the Tathāgata rescues them so that they shall not enter again.
Out of compassion, the World-Honored One preaches the True Dharma for them, pointing out the place of unsurpassed Bodhi for all people.
We do not crave food or drink, nor do we desire worldly wealth and honor, nor do we aspire to be born in the heavens, nor do we fear falling into the evil realms.

Having obtained this human body, we vow to see the World-Honored One; yet sentient beings have short lifespans and wander through the flux of impermanence. Because of their evil karma, they are greedily attached to the five desires and fail to realize that death has arrived; though they know death must come, they feel no dread.
They do not contemplate arising and ceasing, they do not know subtle phenomena, and they do not cultivate subtle karma.
They do not know the realm of quiescence; with their minds shrouded by ignorance, having been born they return to death, and having died they are born again.

The mind likewise does not give rise to thoughts of weary detachment; though suffering for a long night under the torment of being whipped and beaten, it does not conceive weariness or detachment, but instead gives rise to thoughts of plundering, undergoing the suffering of imprisonment and bondage, and being bound by the five fetters.
Due to his past evil karma, as his life-force and consciousness were about to cease, he wept bitterly and said:

"Who will save me? I shall give away all my gold, silver, and various treasures; I am willing to become a slave and perform every kind of labor for you. I have no desire for kingship or self-sovereignty; I require no wealth or goods, I seek only to preserve my life."
"Thus it is, O virtuous one!
We have no need for food or drink.

The exquisite flavors enjoyed by sovereign kings ultimately lead to death; even the nectar-food of the devas returns to extinction. Though there are hundreds of varieties of flavors to which kings are attached, upon seeking their reality, they are found to be non-existent. We have no need for such tastes as food and drink."

We seek to hear the True Dharma so that we may be freed from suffering; may we be released from the bonds of craving and all afflictions of the fetters. We take refuge in the World-Honored One, wishing to be liberated from all bonds.
We pay homage to the Great Sage, the World-Honored One, for the sake of all sentient beings.
We do not yet know what your name is, O Benevolent One;
we pray that you will tell us yourself.
The Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasamudgata said:
"The world is vast; how could one possibly know the names of all sentient beings?
The youths replied:
"We wish to know your name, O Venerable One; we pray that you will proclaim this most profound name.
Bhaiṣajyasamudgata replied, "My name is Bhaiṣajyasamudgata;
I cure the illnesses of sentient beings and am the most supreme among medicines."
I shall now speak for you all, so that you may be free from all illnesses and eliminate the suffering of disease throughout all worlds.
Greed is the great illness of the world; I can extinguish it.
Hatred is a great illness; through it, ignorant sentient beings transmigrate through the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Delusion is a great illness; [the Dharma] can extinguish all the suffering that sentient beings undergo.
The youths said:

"We have heard that by hearing this wondrous Dharma one is freed from all suffering and hardship; ordinary people, lacking wisdom, undergo various afflictions. By hearing this pure Dharma, one is freed from all evil karma; because one is freed from evil karma, there is no fear of the evil realms."
"Quickly go see the Tathāgata, who saves all from illness; he is the King of Physicians who bestows medicine to heal all sufferings.
O Benevolent One, go quickly to pay homage to the Tathāgata and speak our words to the World-Honored One, saying:

'World-Honored One, you can remove our illnesses and extinguish the fires of affliction. The fire of desire burns our bodies and cannot be extinguished; we are in extreme suffering—may the Buddha have compassion for us.'"
"The body is a heavy burden, most terrifying; oppressed by the three poisons, it cannot be overcome.

One constantly carries it throughout coming and going and cannot distance oneself from it. Not knowing that death has arrived, one does not give rise to alarm or fear; one does not know the path to liberation, nor does one know the one who shows the way to liberation."

With a mind clouded by ignorance, they imagine themselves immortal; even upon seeing their parents die, they feel no fear. Their minds are turbid and disordered by various karmas and afflictions as they undergo manifold sufferings—how can they eat?

We are shrouded by ignorance; our minds possess such suffering, along with the aggregates of perception, mental formations, and sensation. Driven by delusion, craving, and lack of wisdom, we transmigrate through the various realms of existence. We give rise to false conceptions in the world and do not recognize liberation.

The people of the world, in their ignorance, bathe with fragrant waters, clothe themselves in superior garments, and partake of the finest flavors. Their ears listen to musical sounds as they indulge in various diversions; they delight in beholding all manner of beautiful forms; their tongues crave and greedily seek every exquisite taste; and their bodies desire to cling to the touch of fine and soft textures.
The deluded mind perceives the union of the two bodies as pleasure; yet where is there any pleasure in this body, which is dull and ignorant?
Even if one is attached to fine shoes, clothing, food, and drink, it is of no avail; when death arrives and suffering reaches its peak, there is no one who can save one.
If one cannot save oneself, how can clothing and other possessions provide salvation?

Living in this world, one drives elephants and horses about, constantly committing evil deeds without seeking liberation; doing so oneself and teaching others to do likewise, one remains ignorant of the retribution that follows.
In our previous existences we had birth, and in this present existence we have death;

there is sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress. We have witnessed the deaths of our parents, brothers, sisters, wives, and children, and we have seen all their grief, mourning, anxiety, and anguish.

All conditioned phenomena are empty; how could a wise person give rise to attachment and delight in them, failing to seek the dharma of quiescence and failing to seek the dharma of liberation from birth and death, with a mind shrouded by craving?
While living in this world, they did not practice giving; among all faults, there is none greater than greed.

Attached to worldly dharmas, they mostly engaged in existence-bound actions, failing to know how to cultivate the path of meditative concentration and liberation, and failing to know how to make great vows to achieve the unsurpassed way.
The Buddha is our father and mother; the Buddha is the one who shows the path to liberation and can rain down benefits upon sentient beings.
When deluded sentient beings do not know how to protect the Dharma, they resolve their minds to seek unsurpassed bodhi—this is called protecting the Dharma.

All conditioned phenomena are empty and material wealth is also empty; if one contemplates the emptiness of the self, one will no longer undergo rebirth. We pray that you, O Benevolent One, out of compassion, will convey our words in full to the Buddha.
For the sake of all bodhisattvas, one should not be indolent regarding the bodhisattva-dharmas, but should diligently cultivate vigor, abandoning evil and practicing good.
O virtuous one, go to the presence of the Buddha on my behalf, pay homage to the Tathāgata, and speak these words:

"World-Honored One, you know all dharmas and have no doubts; the evil Māra and his retinue have already been subdued by the Buddha. The Tathāgata has been able to light the great Dharma-torch so that the masses may obtain happiness. We have never before heard of such a dharma as this which can bring about Buddhahood."

"O Benevolent One, go quickly to where the Buddha is for our sake; we have not yet attained liberation because we have not seen the Tathāgata, whose body is endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics. Only after seeing this body shall we attain liberation."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja said to the youths, "Look upward;
what kind of signs do you see? Having heard this, the people looked upward and saw five hundred transformation Buddhas.

They also saw three thousand great terraces adorned with the seven precious jewels, covered above by nets of the seven precious jewels, from which various fragrances issued forth like the petals of a lotus flower.
Then the sentient beings asked Bhaiṣajyasamudgata,
“What kind of phenomena are these flower seats?
Bhaiṣajyasamudgata replied:
"This is your seat; go quickly to the Buddha's presence to pay homage to the Tathāgata.
The youths replied, "We do not know the path by which to proceed, nor have we seen the Tathāgata; we do not know where to go to pay homage to the Tathāgata."
Bhaiṣajyasamudgata replied:
"Simply pay homage to the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One; just as space and dust have no place of abiding, so too is the Tathāgata."
The Tathāgata’s place of abiding is like Mount Sumeru; the Tathāgata is equal to Mount Sumeru, like the waters of the great ocean.

Bodhisattvas from the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms within a trichiliocosm, seeking the Buddha’s dwelling, do not know its location; the bodhisattvas of the ten directions can only pay him homage from afar.
The youths said, "We pray that your benevolence and kindness may fulfill our wishes; we desire in our hearts to see the Buddha, to draw near to him, and to pay him homage.
Bhaiṣajyarāja replied:

“The Tathāgata does not seek incense or flowers; rather, he acts as a cause for sentient beings to enable them to leave birth and death. He does not engage in contentious debate with the retinues of evil Māras.
Those who take refuge in the Buddha do not enter the gate of death and swiftly attain the Dharma-dhāraṇī.”
"By giving rise to a pure heart and making this vow, you shall immediately behold the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with a voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird, smiled radiantly.
From his face, he emitted eighty-four thousand rays of light, which illuminated the trichiliocosm, reaching downward to the eighteen hells and upward to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

That light was of various colors—blue, yellow, red, white, crystal-colored, and so forth—and such rays issued from the opening of his face, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm; all sentient beings who encountered this light attained peace and happiness.
Having illuminated the world, it returned to the place where the Buddha was, circumambulated the Buddha seven times, and entered through the crown of the Buddha’s head.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I wish to ask a few questions; if the Buddha permits me, I shall venture to speak.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, saying:
"Good son!..."
"In accordance with your questions, the Tathāgata shall analyze and explain them for you, bringing you joy.
Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"These thirty trillion youths wish to hear the subtle and profound Dharma of the Tathāgata; I pray that you will explain it for them.
The Buddha told Bhaiṣajyarāja: "Good son!

If one hears the profound and wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata, they shall awaken to all phenomena and become endowed with all meritorious qualities; on that very day, they will abide in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
They will be able to beat the great Dharma drum and raise the great Dharma banner.
"Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, do you see such a great terrace as this?
Bhaiṣajyasamudgata replied,
"World-Honored One, I do."
“Yes, indeed, I have seen them.
The Buddha told Bhaiṣajyarāja:
“These youths, having today sat upon this terrace, have realized all dharmas and fulfilled all dharmas of the roots of goodness.”
Today I shall strike the great Dharma drum; immeasurable devas and humans, having heard the Dharma, will all obtain benefit.
Immeasurable sentient beings in the hells, having heard the Dharma, will turn their backs on the evil realms.
When these words were spoken, nine thousand koṭis of aged beings within the assembly attained the fruit of srotāpanna.
"Bhaiṣajyasamudgata!
Those who hear this Dharma shall be freed from all suffering and become endowed with all wholesome dharmas."
Bhaiṣajyasamudgata!
All are able to accomplish the Buddha-body.
Bhaiṣajyasamudgata!

“Observe the great Bodhisattvas of the four directions. At that time, Bhaiṣajyarāja immediately observed the four directions. He saw fifty billion Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, coming toward this place from the eastern realm;

he saw sixty billion Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, coming toward this place from the southern realm; he saw seventy billion Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, coming toward this place from the western realm; he saw eighty billion Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, coming toward this place from the northern realm; he saw ninety billion Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, coming toward this place from the downward realm; and he saw ten billion Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, coming toward this place from the upward realm. Having arrived, they all stood to one side before the Buddha.
Bhaiṣajyasamudgata addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What kind of signs are these black and yellow forms seen in the midst of space?”
The Buddha said to Bhaiṣajyasamudgata:
"Do you not know? Bhaiṣajyasamudgata replied to the Buddha:
"Only the Buddha, the Tathāgata, is able to know all things.
The Buddha told Bhaiṣajyarāja:
"This is Māra, the Evil One, together with his retinue, who wishes to come here."
“Bhaiṣajyasamudgata!
Do you wish to see them?
Bhaiṣajyasamudgata addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to see him.
The Buddha then caused Bhaiṣajyarāja to immediately behold the evil Māra.
Having seen this, Bhaiṣajyasamudgata addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition has the evil Māra come here?”
The Buddha told Bhaiṣajyarāja:
"Māra wishes to disturb this Dharma seat.
Bhaiṣajyarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
These bodhisattvas have come because they wish to behold the youths who are receiving their positions.
“O Bhaiṣajyasamudgata!”
"Do you see these bodhisattvas, with their various forms and colors, various appearances, and various powers?
Bhaiṣajyasamudgata addressed the Buddha,
saying, "World-Honored One!"
"Yes, indeed.
I see hundreds of thousands of billions of Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, arriving here by means of their sovereign supernatural powers.

When the World-Honored One had finished preaching this Dharma, the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, all sentient beings—both old and young—and the entire world of devas, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly filled with joy.
